optionExplanations.c: gRPC streams allow a sequence of requests and responses over one call rather than exactly one message each way. Streaming acknowledges communication as an ongoing network interaction.
optionExplanations.d: Exactly-once delivery cannot be guaranteed merely by an RPC framework when requests or responses can be lost. Retries may duplicate execution, and message brokers remain useful for different delivery and buffering needs.

questions.question: What does custom binary RPC win, and what does REST win?

options.text: Binary RPC can be faster, but REST wins on debugging and ecosystem
REST wins on performance; RPC wins on tooling
The two are equivalent in both performance and available tooling
RPC is predominant for public APIs; REST for internal services

questions.explanation: A compact proprietary binary RPC protocol can reduce CPU and bandwidth inside a controlled organization. REST commonly wins at public boundaries because standard HTTP tools, broad client support, readable payloads, and easy debugging matter more than the last increment of wire efficiency.

questions.question: RPC lets you assume an upgrade order that databases cannot. What is that order, and which compatibility do you need where?

options.text: Servers first, then clients — so backward on requests, forward on responses
Clients are updated first, so you need forward compatibility on requests and backward on responses
You need backward compatibility on both requests and responses
You need forward compatibility on both requests and responses

questions.explanation: Servers-first means a new server may read an old client's request (backward) and an old client may read a new server's response (forward). Getting this backwards is the classic error. For evolvability it is important that RPC clients and servers can be changed and deployed independently.

questions.question: 'The backward and forward compatibility properties of an RPC scheme are inherited from whatever encoding it uses.' Spell out the three cases. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Thrift, gRPC (Protocol Buffers) and Avro RPC can be evolved according to the compatibility rules of the respective encoding format
In SOAP, requests and responses are specified with XML schemas, which can be evolved, but there are some subtle pitfalls

RESTful APIs most commonly use JSON without a formally specified schema for responses, and JSON or URI-encoded/form-encoded request parameters for requests; adding optional request parameters and adding new fields to response objects are usually considered changes that maintain compatibility
All RPC schemes have identical compatibility properties regardless of encoding, because compatibility is a property of the transport rather than the schema

questions.explanation: RPC transports do not create compatibility by themselves. Thrift, gRPC, and Avro RPC follow their binary schema rules; SOAP follows XML Schema with its own pitfalls; typical JSON REST APIs rely on conventions such as adding optional request parameters and response fields.

optionExplanations.a: Thrift, Protocol Buffers used by gRPC, and Avro RPC inherit the add/remove/type rules of their respective schemas. The transport does not override those byte-format semantics.
optionExplanations.b: SOAP messages follow XML schemas, which can evolve but contain subtle compatibility traps around optionality, ordering, and generated bindings. A standardized envelope does not eliminate schema design.
optionExplanations.c: Typical JSON REST APIs rely on conventions rather than one formal response schema: adding optional request parameters or response fields is usually tolerated. Clients must still ignore what they do not understand.
optionExplanations.d: Compatibility is determined by how requests and responses are encoded and interpreted, not by the fact that all travel over a transport. Different schema systems therefore expose different safe changes.

questions.question: What makes service compatibility harder than database compatibility?

options.text: Clients are often outside your control, so compatibility must last indefinitely
Services carry far more data per request than a database does, so old formats linger
Service protocols change faster than storage formats, so breaks happen more often
Services cannot use schema registries, so there is nowhere to record a version

questions.explanation: Database readers are usually deployed by the same organization that owns the data, so obsolete code can eventually be retired. Service clients may belong to customers or partners and remain unupdated indefinitely, forcing the provider to preserve old request and response contracts much longer.

questions.question: How is API versioning handled?

options.text: There is no agreement; version numbers appear in URLs or Accept headers
Versioning is standardized: the version always goes in the URL
Versioning is handled automatically by HTTP content negotiation
API versioning is unnecessary if the encoding is compatible

questions.explanation: There is no universal API-versioning convention. Some services place a version in the URL, others negotiate it through `Accept` headers, and some use administrative mechanisms to select a version. Compatible evolution can reduce version proliferation but does not eliminate the need for policy.

questions.question: How does brokered asynchronous messaging combine properties of RPC and databases?

options.text: A broker stores messages temporarily while still aiming for low-latency delivery
A proxy forwards synchronous calls without retaining any message data
A database keeps messages permanently for arbitrary ad hoc querying
Peers exchange messages directly with no intermediary or buffering

questions.explanation: Like RPC, messages are normally delivered soon; like a database, an intermediary stores bytes until another process reads them. The broker or message queue buffers load and decouples sender availability from recipient availability.

questions.question: Which advantages does a message broker have over direct RPC? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It can act as a buffer if the recipient is unavailable or overloaded, and thus improve system reliability
It can automatically redeliver messages to a process that has crashed, and thus prevent messages from being lost

It avoids the sender needing to know the IP address and port number of the recipient, which is particularly useful in a cloud deployment where virtual machines often come and go; and it allows one message to be sent to several recipients
It guarantees that messages are delivered to consumers in exactly the order the sender produced them, which a direct RPC call cannot promise across retries

questions.explanation: A broker can buffer while recipients are unavailable, redeliver after consumer failure, hide changing network locations, fan one message out to several consumers, and decouple producers from consumer identity. Ordering guarantees vary by broker and configuration, so they are not automatic.

optionExplanations.a: A broker persists or buffers messages while a recipient is down or overloaded, letting producers continue temporarily. This decouples availability and smooths bursts.
optionExplanations.b: If a consumer crashes before acknowledging work, a broker can offer the message again to another or restarted consumer. Redelivery reduces loss but may create duplicates that consumers must handle.
optionExplanations.c: Producers address a stable queue or topic rather than a changing host, and publish-subscribe can fan one message to several recipients. This decouples identity and network location.
optionExplanations.d: Ordering depends on partitions, concurrency, retries, and broker configuration; it is not universally exact. Direct RPC also has ordering nuances, so an unconditional broker guarantee is false.

questions.question: How does message-passing communication differ from RPC in direction, and what does 'asynchronous' mean here?

options.text: Usually one-way and asynchronous — send and forget, with replies on another channel
It is bidirectional and synchronous, so the sender blocks until a reply arrives
It is one-way but synchronous, blocking the sender until delivery is confirmed
It is identical to RPC in both direction and timing, differing only in encoding

questions.explanation: A producer normally publishes and continues without waiting for the consumer to process the message or return a value. If a reply is needed, it arrives later through another queue or topic, making the interaction one-way at each step rather than a blocking request/response call.

questions.question: Name the commercial and open source message brokers in common use, and describe the usage model. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Message brokers used to be dominated by commercial enterprise software from TIBCO, IBM WebSphere and webMethods; more recently open source implementations such as RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, NATS and Apache Kafka have become popular

One process sends a message to a named queue or topic, and the broker ensures that the message is delivered to one or more consumers of or subscribers to that topic; there can be many producers and many consumers on the same topic

A topic provides only one-way dataflow, but a consumer may itself publish messages to another topic, or to a reply queue that is consumed by the sender of the original message — allowing a request/response dataflow similar to RPC
Brokers impose a particular data model, so every message must be encoded as JSON before it can be published to a topic

questions.explanation: A broker treats a message as bytes plus metadata and does not impose JSON or any other data model. Publishers and consumers can therefore choose an encoding; using one with backward and forward compatibility lets the two sides evolve independently. Delivery guarantees depend on implementation and configuration.

optionExplanations.a: The listed commercial systems and later open-source brokers describe the ecosystem's evolution. TIBCO, WebSphere, and webMethods preceded broad adoption of RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, NATS, and Kafka.
optionExplanations.b: Queues and topics let many producers publish independently and one or more consumers subscribe. The broker owns delivery routing rather than requiring direct producer-to-consumer connections.
optionExplanations.c: Each topic flow is one-way, but a consumer can publish a later result to another topic or reply queue. Chaining one-way messages can therefore construct asynchronous request-response patterns.
optionExplanations.d: Brokers carry bytes plus metadata and generally do not require JSON or one application data model. Producers and consumers may choose Avro, Protobuf, JSON, or another compatible encoding.

questions.question: Define the actor model.

options.text: A concurrency model where logic lives in actors with private state and async messages
A model in which all state is shared between threads and protected by explicit locks
A model for distributed transactions across nodes with guaranteed message delivery
A model where each thread owns one message queue with guaranteed global ordering

questions.explanation: Crucially, delivery is not guaranteed even within a single process — which is what makes the distributed case less of a leap.

questions.question: Why does location transparency work better in the actor model than in RPC?

options.text: Because the model already assumes messages may be lost, even locally
Because actor frameworks guarantee delivery over the network
Because actors run only on a single node
Because network latency is lower than local message passing

questions.explanation: Actors already communicate through asynchronous messages that may be delayed or lost even within one process. Moving the recipient to another node therefore changes latency and encoding, but not the fundamental programming model as radically as turning a reliable-looking local function call into RPC.

questions.question: How can Orleans handle a rolling upgrade when its default actor encoding is incompatible?

options.text: Shift traffic to a parallel cluster or install a compatible serializer plug-in
Restart every actor simultaneously and discard all queued messages
Rely on the default format to become compatible without configuration
Convert all actor messages to untyped JSON at the network boundary

questions.explanation: Orleans can use a custom serializer or move clients gradually to a new cluster. Akka likewise can replace Java serialization with a schema-evolvable format. Erlang supports rolling code upgrades, but record-shape changes still require planning; framework support does not eliminate encoding compatibility work.

questions.question: Which benefits do rolling upgrades bring? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A new version of a service is gradually deployed to a few nodes at a time, rather than deploying to all nodes simultaneously
Releases can be made without downtime, thus encouraging frequent small releases over rare big releases
Deployments are made less risky, allowing faulty releases to be detected and rolled back before they affect a large number of users
They remove the need for backward and forward compatibility, since all nodes run one version

questions.explanation: Rolling upgrades replace only some nodes at a time, avoiding downtime and limiting the impact of a faulty release. They also mean old and new code coexist, so new code must read old data and old code must read new data; deployment safety increases the need for both compatibility directions.

optionExplanations.a: Replacing a few nodes at a time limits simultaneous change and allows the old fleet to continue serving traffic. Operators can observe the new version before expanding deployment.
optionExplanations.b: Because old nodes remain available while new ones start, releases need not require a service-wide outage. Lower deployment cost encourages smaller, more frequent changes.
optionExplanations.c: A faulty build affects only the initial subset and can be stopped or rolled back before most users encounter it. Gradual exposure reduces blast radius.
optionExplanations.d: Rolling deployment deliberately creates a period when old and new versions run together. That coexistence increases the need for backward and forward compatibility rather than removing it.

questions.question: Which encoding family combines compact data with explicit schema-evolution rules?

options.text: Schema-driven binary formats such as Avro or Protocol Buffers
Language-specific native object serialization formats
Schemaless text formats such as JSON, XML, or CSV
Ad hoc positional binary records with no schema

questions.explanation: Language-specific encodings are convenient but couple data to one runtime and are often unsafe for long-lived exchange. Text formats are broadly interoperable but vague about types and compatibility. Schema-driven binary formats add compactness and defined evolution rules, at the cost of managing schemas.

questions.question: Restate the three dataflow modes in which encoding matters.

options.text: Databases, REST and RPC APIs, and asynchronous message passing
Storage, compute and network; the final line is about performance
Batch, stream and interactive; the final line is about correctness
Client, server and broker; the final line warns against rolling upgrades

questions.explanation: Each mode is defined by who encodes and who decodes, which is exactly the relationship compatibility governs.
